newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB's Gehrig sees easier Swiss franc - paper.
newsitem.headline: SNB's Gehrig sees easier Swiss franc - paper.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) expects the Swiss franc to weaken slightly as the effects of its recent cut in the discount rate is not yet fully reflected in the franc's exchange rate, SNB board member Bruno Gehrig said.

Gehrig also told the Swiss financial bi-weekly Finanz und Wirtschaft (F&W) that there was still some scepticism in the market over whether the SNB would continue its recent flexible money market policy.
The interview with Gehrig was provided to Reuters ahead of publication on Wednesday.

"Without doubt there is scepticism in the market about whether the SNB will continue the flexible money market policy that it started this summer. If we continue, this conviction will take hold in the market," Gehrig said.
"I expect a further slight weakening because the franc is, however I measure it, overvalued in real terms," he added.
A SNB spokesman confirmed Gehrig's statements and said the interview had taken place last Thursday.
The SNB cut its discount rate by 50 basis points to 1.00 percent on September 26. Since late July the SNB has been generous with liquidity in money markets.
Gehrig said some banks had not expected the SNB to continue its policy of supplying the money markets generously.

However, the cut in the discount rate was a clear signal that the SNB wanted money market rates temporarily to remain at a low level and market participants will also have to adjust to that situation, he said.
"It is difficult to judge how far the expectations already are contained in the exchange rate and how fast expectations still have to adapt," Gehrig said, adding:
"But the basis for a further slight weakening of the franc has been laid."
The SNB's cut in its discount rate was seen by some economists as a sign that the central bank was looking to the exchange rate as a guide to monetary policy.

Gehrig said the SNB had often repeated that it does not conduct an exchange rate policy with exchange rate targets in mind. Those statements, however, have been interpreted as showing the SNB was indifferent to exchange rates.

"That interpretation is false. The exchange rate is an significant element in the financial sitution that is part of our decision-making process -- even if the exchange rate is not the monetary aim of our efforts," he said.
But Gehrig added that a shift in emphasis had taken place in that the SNB had scope to be expansive in its monetary policy without triggering inflation.
Shifting to the introduction of Europe's single currency, the Euro, Gehrig said this would lead to a change in the composition of currencies traded.
"I can imagine that the SNB would accumulate the Euro as a reserve currency," he said.
When demand for the Euro starts taking shape, Gehrig said demand for Swiss francs has been analysed carefully.
"It is conceivable that foreign central banks want to hold more francs as currency reserve," Gehrig said, adding he also expected shifts in private portfolios.

He said the SNB would observe this development so it could react if necessary. The strength of the currency diversification would depend on how the Euro is able to establish itself as a investment currency, Gehrig added.
